title: Predicted bird extinctions shifts morphological diversity in a metropolitan region in Eastern Amazon
content:
Abstract

Understanding how local extinctions caused by urbanization affects the distribution of functional traits within natural communities can provide essential information for biodiversity conservation within urban ecosystems. This is especially urgent in the tropics, where urban areas are often surrounded by highly diverse tropical forests. Here, we assess if bird extinctions in the Belém Metropolitan Region (BMR), Eastern Amazon, have altered the morphological space of the regional bird community. We first gathered bird occurrence records and local extinction events from the literature for the BMR (527 recorded species). We then compiled morphological data for the BMR bird species based on nine morphological traits measured across 3,250 individual birds. Morphological diversity (MD) metrics were then used to compare observed values with expectations based on random and probabilistic extinction scenarios. Our results suggest that bird extinctions within the BMR removed species with specialized traits that occurred along the periphery of the morphological space, resulting in significant losses in MD, even when a small number of species disappeared. Simulated extinction events revealed a strictly decreasing monotonic relationship between MD and species richness, indicating that the BMR may lose even more MD with accumulated local extinctions. Taken together, our results indicate bird extinctions within the BMR have significantly affected the region’s MD through the removal of species with unique morphologies. The loss of the ecosystem services provided by these species could have broad implications for region’s biodiversity.
